item.title: Comment on Gradual Empowerment? by mento
item.description:
The word " collusion " is not in the paper. Collusion is not necessary for the argument. Competition could lead AI to strategies that disadvantage humans.

Advanced AIs might find it easier to communicate and coordinate with each other than humans do, because they exchange and process data at superhuman speed. That doesn’t require a big pre-agreed plan; it may arise from the systems responding to similar incentives or recognizing each other as “peers” with shared strategic interests.

“Checks and balances” might exist among AIs themselves, but not necessarily in a way that preserves human autonomy or safety. If multiple advanced AIs constantly fight or sabotage each other, that can be very detrimental to humans — and we might have little say in the outcome.

The paper describes a world perhaps far from now , where humans are simply out of the loop, Ais mostly communicate with each other, make all the economic decisions, run the firms and humans make no economic or intellectual contribution. Humans end up mostly trusting them because we don’t have the intellectual power to understand them, let alone counter or thwart them. Humans are relegated to a human centric sub-culture, perhaps dominated by entertainment that becomes more and more irrelevant to an AI dominated world even if the AIs have no plans to take over.

From the paper:
“If these systems become less reliant on human labor and cognition, that would also decrease the extent to which humans could explicitly or implicitly align them. As a result, these systems—and the outcomes they produce—might drift further from providing what humans want.

Isn't that the scenario where we diverged from chimps ( genetically , culturally) but on a much much compressed time frame; the AI culture becomes incredibly cognitive and a split occurs over time that cannot be bridged.

item.title: Comment on Monday assorted links by Sure
item.description:
Reply to Alan Wright:

#5. "Don't Believe Him." - a helpful essay. The question, however, is whether and how many people and politicians will oppose the Trump/ Musk power grab.

The progressive left has already been standing up. The moderates less so.

What about civil libertarians? History will likely prove both Trump and Musk have elfar exceeded their lawful authority relative to (a) Congress and (b) impoundment, and all many of legal and regulatory safeguards.

(I need not mention the 2nd Amendment rights people. One of their stated purposes for their gun rights was to oppose government overreach and the slippery slope toward tyranny. Yet their seem silent with this version of the unitary executive.)

Spare me. The measure of actual opposition to Trump is how much groups are willing to defy their own interests to limit the reach of Trump.

Progressives could have made common cause with their opponents to limit Trump.

"We support abortion rights, but we understand that our opponents think it should be left to the states, so we are going to fight the battle there rather than have Joe Biden buck supermajority opposition to repeal Mexico City - Democracy is too important to had red meat to the swing pro-life voters"

"We believe in trans-rights, but as hard as it might be, now is not the time for a federal push. The federal government must be studiously neutral at this time with respect to sports participation. The federal prisons will limit reassignment of prisoners to those who have undergone genital surgery out of respect for concerns about female safety."

"America is a nation of immigrants and we don't think it is worth the effort to deport people here who are net contributors and law abiding, but we will depart everyone who gets a parking ticket to calm the fears of the swing voters on immigration."

"Inflation kills presidencies, so we should limit our spending at the federal level on issues not salient with the electorate. Climate change is important, but large outlays now risk spiking inflation and Trump is simply too dangerous to the climate to risk rapid spending now."

Progressives had four years to make sacrifices to Trump-proof the election. They did nothing. They went so far as to try to hold popular infrastructure spending hostage because Joe Manchin - senator for the most Trump happy state in the union - was unwilling to cut a blank cheque to fund progressive wish lists.

How about the civil liberties groups? The ACLU opted not to support the Observant Christian who opposes gay marriage and Halloween. They formally subordinated defending free speech to maintaining "relationships with allies or coalition partners". At least they made passing nods to the NRA and Trump on gag orders ... but far too often the leadership was more concerned with advancing progressivism rather than defending civil rights as such.

And, of course, the best protection against a unitary executive is legislative. And of course, I recall nary a peep from these groups when they actually had leverage to pass any.

And, of course, after having watched endless reruns of Democrats saying they lacked the power to enact DACA extra-legislatively or to forgive student loans repeatedly after being repeatedly told by the courts that this is unconstitutional ... I am not expecting unilateral disarmament now.

A bunch of opportunistic opponents to the unitary executive who just so happen to be advocating for restraint and legislative supremacy exactly when such is to the immediate benefit of their cause is simply too little too late.

And I fully expect the Republicans to fail the test of the Trump years. The executive will march further forward and because it helps their cause in the moment, the right folks will let procedure and norms falter blindgly.

Frankly, my expectation is that power blocs will only make the necessary sacrifices to their own sides when forced to do so. Maybe one side wins for long enough for them to legislate their victories and protect them from executive meddling. Maybe things get violent and concessions are finally mutual as everyone is terrified of things getting worse. Maybe Republicans (or Democrats) get locked out of power for four sequential elections and finally commit to restraint as a necessary precondition of being competitive in the 2032 electoral college.

But be serious here. Clinton, Bush, Obama, Trump, Biden, and now Trump again has resulted in everyone using ever expanding presidential powers whenever they can. Anybody whole was not consistently arguing for limitations in '13, '17, and '21 can generally be assumed to be disingenuous until they offer explicit quid pro quos where they sacrifice things of real value to them. And sadly, so far this looks like ... everyone.
